title: Winning Over Peers Before You Need Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post takes up influencing without authority, the challenge of getting peers and distant colleagues to collaborate when they owe you nothing. Peers are busy and silently ask what is in it for them, so the author argues the strongest asset a leader can offer is useful information. The essential move is timing: supply peers with data, updates and trend summaries before any request is made. This builds goodwill and invokes reciprocity, so that help is offered when it is finally needed. The post frames the habit as a deliberate strategy that the best leaders and team members practice.
points: Peers outside the immediate team range from helpful to openly competitive, and influence without formal authority is a permanent feature of organizational life.
Peers are usually asking what's in it for me, and critical information is among the most attractive things a leader can offer.
The key move is sharing valuable information with peers before any request exists.
Reciprocity makes peers more willing to help because they know you did not have to keep them so well informed.
Leaders can create metrics, uncover data and summarize trends specifically for the peers they will later need.
quotes: Peer relationships outside of the immediate team are complex. Some peers will go out of their way to help when they can, while others view their organizational colleagues as competitors who diminish their share of resources and rewards.
Influencing without authority, as it is often called, remains a frustrating and perplexing reality of organizational life. And it’s not going away.

As a rule, peers are busy with their own work and are reluctant to offer assistance when they don’t have to. When faced with a request to collaborate or lend a hand, peers typically have a central question in the back of their minds: What’s in it for me?

Finding and sharing information with peers before you need them is the essential move. Keeping them on a steady diet of information valuable to them before any requests or needs arise sets the stage and develops a stronger relationship.

Then, when the time comes, peers are more likely to lend a hand because they know you didn’t have to keep them so well-informed. Reciprocity is a powerful human motivator and peers are not immune to it.

The best leaders and team members feed peers the information they need, want, and crave. They go out of their way to create metrics, uncover data, provide updates, and summarize trends they suspect their peers will value. In so doing, they prime the pump of goodwill.
